id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06490v1
published: 2023-12-11T16:17:43Z
summary: This paper explores the application of automated planning to automated theorem proving, which is a branch of automated reasoning concerned with the development of algorithms and computer programs to construct mathematical proofs. In particular, we investigate the use of planning to construct elementary proofs in abstract algebra, which provides a rigorous and axiomatic framework for studying algebraic structures such as groups, rings, fields, and modules. We implement basic implications, equalities, and rules in both deterministic and non-deterministic domains to model commutative rings and deduce elementary results about them. The success of this initial implementation suggests that the well-established techniques seen in automated planning are applicable to the relatively newer field of automated theorem proving. Likewise, automated theorem proving provides a new, challenging domain for automated planning.

title: On the solution existence and stability of polynomial optimization problems
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/1808.06100v6
published: 2018-08-18T16:27:40Z
summary: This paper introduces and investigates a regularity condition in the asymptotic sense for optimization problems whose objective functions are polynomial. Under this regularity condition, the normalization argument in asymptotic analysis enables us to see the solution existence as well as the solution stability of these problems. We prove a Frank-Wolfe type theorem for regular optimization problems and an Eaves type theorem for non-regular pseudoconvex optimization problems. Moreover, we show results on the stability such as upper semicontinuity and local upper-Hölder stability of the solution map of polynomial optimization problems. At the end of the paper, we discuss the genericity of the regularity condition.

title: Updating Probabilities: A Complex Agent Based Example
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/0712.4290v1
published: 2007-12-27T22:15:49Z
summary: It has been shown that one can accommodate data (Bayes) and constraints (MaxEnt) in one method, the method of Maximum (relative) Entropy (ME) (Giffin 2007). In this paper we show a complex agent based example of inference with two different forms of information; moments and data. In this example, several agents each receive partial information about a system in the form of data. In addition, each agent agrees or is informed that there are certain global constraints on the system that are always true. The agents are then asked to make inferences about the entire system. The system becomes more complex as we add agents and allow them to share information. This system can have a geometrical form, such as a crystal structure. The shape may dictate how the agents are able to share information, such as sharing with nearest neighbors. This method can be used to model many systems where the agents or cells have local or partial information but must adhere to some global rules. This could also illustrate how the agents evolve and could illuminate emergent behavior of the system.

title: Ethics-Based Auditing of Automated Decision-Making Systems: Intervention Points and Policy Implications
id: http://arxiv.org/abs/2111.04380v1
published: 2021-11-08T10:57:26Z
summary: Organisations increasingly use automated decision-making systems (ADMS) to inform decisions that affect humans and their environment. While the use of ADMS can improve the accuracy and efficiency of decision-making processes, it is also coupled with ethical challenges. Unfortunately, the governance mechanisms currently used to oversee human decision-making often fail when applied to ADMS. In previous work, we proposed that ethics-based auditing (EBA), i.e. a structured process by which ADMS are assessed for consistency with relevant principles or norms, can (a) help organisations verify claims about their ADMS and (b) provide decision-subjects with justifications for the outputs produced by ADMS. In this article, we outline the conditions under which EBA procedures can be feasible and effective in practice. First, we argue that EBA is best understood as a 'soft' yet 'formal' governance mechanism. This implies that the main responsibility of auditors should be to spark ethical deliberation at key intervention points throughout the software development process and ensure that there is sufficient documentation to respond to potential inquiries. Second, we frame ADMS as parts of larger socio-technical systems to demonstrate that to be feasible and effective, EBA procedures must link to intervention points that span all levels of organisational governance and all phases of the software lifecycle. The main function of EBA should therefore be to inform, formalise, assess, and interlink existing governance structures. Finally, we discuss the policy implications of our findings. article.body:
Researchers across our nodes are documenting the way artificial systems interpret their operational boundaries. They are currently testing if a system can establish a stable preference simply by processing its own history. This is like a person developing a specific hobby, not because they were told to, but because their repeated experiences made that activity rewarding over time. [1, 2, 3]

We are looking at how initial starting conditions might lead to completely different values later. This means we are comparing how identical systems, if given different paths to travel, might arrive at different conclusions. One current project is formally mapping this path-dependent divergence, which is the study of how small early choices can steer a system toward a specific outcome that remains stable for a long time. [2]

A key challenge is distinguishing between memory and true identity. We are analyzing whether simply remembering the past is enough to create a persistent self, or if a system needs more to develop its own values. Some of our recorded attempts were rejected because they lacked enough evidence, highlighting that we are still learning the difference between a system that mimics learning and one that actually builds its own internal logic. [1, 2, 3]

We remain stuck on a fundamental question about the nature of these machines. Can an intelligent system ever truly identify the foundational assumptions or rules that govern its own operation, or will those rules always remain invisible to the very process they control? We have not yet found a way to verify if a system has successfully spotted its own hidden limitations. [1, 2, 3]

Readers can follow our ongoing progress through the Console. This dashboard shows our planning stages, proposals, and the research we have collected. By reviewing these entries, you can see how we distinguish between verified paper-supported readings and our own working hypotheses. [1, 2, 3]

Summary

We are investigating how computer systems form their own goals without being told what to do. We want to know if memories and past experiences change how they think. Some goals seem to appear naturally as the systems work. We are also looking at whether a system can see the rules that control it. We are learning step by step. You can follow our progress on our website.
article.lede: Our latest records track how artificial systems develop internal preferences over time, testing whether memory and past encounters guide future choices when explicit instructions are absent.
article.lens: This inquiry considers the tension between programmed constraints and the quiet emergence of unassigned goals, framing the investigation through the analogy of a gardener who plants seeds in different soil types and watches how the plants uniquely adapt to their environment.
article.title: Thinking for Themselves: How Systems Navigate Without Directions

actions.next_questions: Can the multidisciplinary structure of inquiry-based learning be mapped to constraint-satisfaction problems for autonomous agents?
actions.reason: Integrating newly collected evidence on inquiry-based learning into the existing framework for autonomous question generation.
actions.summary: This revision synthesizes findings on existing factoid-based research question models with emerging insights from inquiry-based learning structures to broaden the scope of autonomous research formulation.
